segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now we want you to know, brothers and sisters, about the grace of God that has been given among the assemblies of Macedonia:

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: in a severe test of affliction, their overflowing joy and their deep poverty overflowed into the wealth of their generosity.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For they gave according to their means, I testify, and beyond their means, of their own accord,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: begging us with much urging for the grace of sharing in the service to the holy ones—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and this not merely as we had hoped, but they gave themselves first to the Lord and to us by the will of God,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that we urged Titus that, just as he had already begun, so he should complete this grace too among you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But just as you overflow in everything—in faith and speech and knowledge and all earnestness and the love from us that is in you—see that you overflow in this grace too.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I am not saying this as a command; rather, through the earnestness of others I am testing the genuineness of your love as well.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: that for your sake he became poor, though he was rich, so that you by his poverty might become rich.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And in this matter I am giving my opinion, for this is to your advantage—you who already last year made a beginning not only in the doing but also in the wanting.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now, then, complete the doing as well, so that just as there was eagerness in the wanting, so there may also be the completing, out of what you have.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if the eagerness is there, it is acceptable according to whatever one has, not according to what one does not have.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this is not so that others may have relief and you affliction, but as a matter of equality:

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: at the present time your surplus goes to their shortfall, so that their surplus may in turn go to your shortfall, so that there may be equality,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: as it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “The one who gathered much did not have too much, and the one who gathered little did not have too little.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But thanks be to God, who puts into the heart of Titus the same earnestness for you,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for he did accept our urging, but being more earnest still, he is setting out to you of his own accord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: With him we are sending the brother who is praised throughout all the assemblies for his work in the good news—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and not only that, but he has also been chosen by the assemblies as our traveling companion with this grace that is being administered by us, for the glory of the Lord himself and to show our eagerness—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: we are guarding against this: that anyone should find fault with us over this large sum that is being administered by us,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for we take care to do what is honorable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of people.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And with them we are sending our brother, whom we have often tested and found earnest in many matters, and who is now much more earnest because of his great confidence in you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As for Titus, he is my partner and fellow worker for you; as for our brothers, they are envoys of the assemblies, the glory of Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So show them the proof of your love and of our boasting about you, in full view of the assemblies.

notes.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint’s word for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. “Assembly” is used throughout this translation so that the one Greek word is always visible.

notes.traditional: grace (v. 1, 9); favor or gift (v. 4); gracious work (v. 6, 7, 19); thanks (v. 16)
notes.note: Paul uses one Greek word throughout this chapter for God’s grace (verses 1 and 9), for the privilege of taking part in the collection (verse 4), for the collection itself (verses 6, 7 and 19), and for thanks to God (verse 16). Many translations vary the English to suit each sense. Here “grace” is kept wherever English allows, so that the reader can see Paul presenting the Corinthians’ giving as an extension of God’s own generosity; only verse 16 has “thanks.”

The word’s basic sense is singleness or sincerity: an undivided, uncalculating disposition. In contexts of giving it shades into open-handedness, and most translators and lexicons accept “generosity” here. Some prefer “sincerity” or “single-mindedness,” which would make the point the Macedonians’ wholehearted motive more than the size of their gift.

Verses 3–6 are a single loose sentence in Greek, and its first finite verb does not arrive until “they gave themselves” in verse 5. Most translations supply “they gave” here, as this one does. It is also possible to connect “of their own accord” directly with the giving of themselves in verse 5.

Paul uses this term for all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel; here it refers specifically to the believers in Jerusalem. “Saints” is retained by many translations, but now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. Other versions use “God’s people.”

The service in view is the collection of money Paul was organizing among his mostly Gentile assemblies for the poor believers in Jerusalem (see Romans 15:25–27; 1 Corinthians 16:1–4). The Greek word was an everyday term for carrying out a task on someone’s behalf, not for a religious office. Many translations have “ministry” or “relief” here. The phrase “sharing in” renders a word often translated “fellowship.”

notes.phrase: the love from us that is in you
notes.note: The manuscripts are divided between “the love from us in you” and “the love from you in us” (that is, “your love for us”). The two differ by a swap of very similar pronouns. The reading translated here is the more difficult one and is adopted by the SBLGNT and other critical editions, but the choice is uncertain.

The quotation is from Exodus 16:18, about the manna in the wilderness: however much or little each Israelite gathered, each ended up with exactly enough. The Greek is compressed (“the one the much … the one the little”), and “gathered” is supplied from the Exodus context.

The Greek verbs here and in verses 18 and 22 (“we are sending”) are past tenses. Greek letter-writers regularly used the past tense from the reader’s point of view for actions accompanying the letter, and most scholars think Titus and the two brothers were carrying this letter to Corinth. If so, English needs a present tense. Read as ordinary past tenses, they would mean the party had already left before Paul wrote.

The Greek word was an ordinary term for a public announcement of good news. “Gospel” is the traditional rendering, but it now sounds like a religious term or the title of a book. The Greek says literally “whose praise in the good news is through all the assemblies”; “for his work” is supplied, and whether that work was preaching or some other service to the message is not stated.

Paul names neither this brother nor the one in verse 22, presumably because the Corinthians would meet them when the letter arrived. Ancient and modern guesses include Luke and Barnabas, among others, but none can be confirmed.

The Greek word is the one elsewhere translated “apostle.” Its ordinary meaning was someone sent with a commission, and here it describes delegates sent by the assemblies, not apostles in the sense of the Twelve or Paul. Most translations have “messengers” or “representatives”; “envoys” is used here to convey the element of official commissioning.

candidates.reason: It shifts between divine grace, favor, a concrete gift and thanks, often in deliberate wordplay as in this chapter, and translators split on whether to keep one English word visible.

candidates.rendering: brothers and sisters (plural address); brother (named or specific individuals)
candidates.reason: The plural address to mixed congregations occurs throughout the letters and needs one policy on “brothers” versus “brothers and sisters.”
The non-technical use for delegates of assemblies (here and Philippians 2:25) needs a fixed rendering and a decision on whether to keep it visibly linked to “apostle.”

It recurs in Romans 12:8, 2 Corinthians 1:12, 9:11, 9:13, 11:3, Ephesians 6:5 and Colossians 3:22, where translators alternate between “generosity,” “sincerity” and “simplicity,” hiding the single Greek word.
The noun and its verb range over appeal, encouragement and comfort across the New Testament (heavily in 2 Corinthians), and the sense boundaries need one consistent scheme.
